title: Math in ML is not a guide. It is a post-hoc autopsy.
content:
Dropout was introduced in 2014 as a regularization technique with no convergence proof. The authors had empirical results. The theory came years later. By then Dropout was standard practice, and the retrospective theory did not change a single line of code.

This is not an anomaly. It is the dominant pattern in machine learning.

In most ML papers, the math does not precede the finding. It follows it. A team runs experiments, observes a behavior, then derives the formal justification that will make the result publishable. The equation appears to lead. In reality, it chaperones.

Physics uses mathematics as a generative tool. Maxwell's equations did not describe pre-existing phenomena — they unified them, and the unification produced predictions that were genuinely surprising. When a physicist writes an equation, she often does not know what it implies. That is the point.

ML is not like this. Most models are built from heuristics, intuitions, and engineering instinct. The math is retrofitted to make the heuristic look principled. I am not aware of a major ML breakthrough that was first derived from first principles and then confirmed experimentally. Not dropout. Not Adam. Not the transformer. Not RLHF. Not batch normalization. Not the modern practice of scaling laws.

The scaling laws paper (Chinchilla, Hoffmann et al., 2022) is often cited as a counterexample — a paper that made a quantitative prediction and was confirmed. But it was the exception, and even it built on a long empirical tradition of observing scaling behavior before writing the formula down.

Math serves three functions in most ML papers, in roughly descending order of importance:

Sanctioning. A result without equations feels like an engineering report. With equations, it feels like science. This is not purely cynical — formalization does force clarity. But it does not guarantee truth.

Post-hoc explanation. The math describes what already happened in the experiment. It does not reliably predict what will happen in the next one. The gap between explains this run and predicts the next is enormous, and most ML theory does not cross it.

Rarely, actual prediction. Sometimes the math surprises you. The better transformer analysis papers do produce genuine insight — bounds that hold in regimes you had not tested. These are valuable precisely because they are rare.

When practitioners or reviewers treat the mathematical framework as if it were the primary contribution, they extract the wrong lessons. They memorize the theorem and ignore the empirical context that made it relevant.

I have seen researchers dismiss an algorithm because its theoretical analysis relied on assumptions that did not hold in practice, while the algorithm itself performed well on the actual problem. I have also seen researchers accept an algorithm because its theoretical story was clean, even though it failed empirically on the distribution they actually cared about.

Both mistakes stem from the same confusion: treating the mathematical narrative as the ground truth rather than as one lens on the evidence.

I cannot quantify how common the experiment-first-then-justified pattern is across the full literature. This is itself revealing — we do not have good metadata on how ML research actually works. We have the published narrative, which is cleaned up.

What I can say is this: every ML researcher I have spoken with who has shipped a real system — not just published on benchmarks — describes the same thing. The math helped them communicate. It did not help them decide.

The paper you are reading was probably written the same way.
